Roamly Groups: Go-to-Market Strategy

Help existing Roamly customers turn an idea for one local activity with friends into completed bookings, with each attendee managing their own participation and payment.

Bob Steeger | Go-to-Market | November 2–23, 2026

View the repo →
What I built

Five modules, one go-to-market plan

Each module added one decision. Together they set who Roamly Groups is for, how it wins and how it makes money.

Module 1
GTM strategy

Full GTM strategy

Target segment

Existing Roamly customers informally organizing one local activity with friends. Start with customers showing group-booking intent or reporting coordination friction. Professional organizers and corporate groups are outside the initial scope.

GTM motion

Product-led growth: introduce Groups at relevant planning and booking steps, recruit pilot users through Support, re-engage known group intent through targeted email, and make invitations easy to complete. Measure participation before treating invitations as a repeatable acquisition channel.

Primary goal

Expand booking activity among existing customers by converting more attempted group bookings into confirmed bookings. Establish a baseline and conversion window before setting an improvement target. Track abandonment, attendee participation and support contacts; new customer acquisition and longer-term retention are secondary outcomes to investigate.

Module 2
Battlecard and strategic bet

Full battlecard and strategic bet

Primary competitor

Airbnb Experiences

Strategic bet

I am betting that Roamly Groups wins by making it simple for a coordinator to propose an experience and invite others, then letting each participant join, select their options, and pay for their own selections.

Deprioritizing

To make this bet, I am deprioritizing professional travel organizers and corporate groups, whose workflows and commercial needs would require a different approach. I’ll focus first on individual travelers bringing friends together for shared local experiences.

Module 3
Positioning

Full positioning framework and pressure test

Target audience

The friend in the group chat who suggests one local activity, such as the kayak on Saturday, and wants a few friends there without becoming the person who runs it.

Positioning statement

Roamly Groups coordinates one local activity with friends. The person who starts the plan brings the group together, and each person takes their own spot, changes it, drops it, and pays on their own card. Changes and cancellations remain subject to host rules, capacity and deadlines.

Module 4
Messaging pillars

Full messaging pillars and asset review

From/To shift

From: The person who suggests an activity becomes everyone’s coordinator—inviting friends, finding a shared date, making bookings, and collecting money, sometimes paying upfront and chasing reimbursement. To: The initiator shares an idea and invites friends. Each friend indicates availability so the group can settle on a shared date, selects their activity options, and books and pays for their own participation.

Audience pillars

Initiators
Value: Bring friends together while saving time and energy and avoiding coordination frustration.
Capabilities: Invitations and a guided group flow for availability, a shared date, options, individual booking and payment.
Evidence: Estimated current burden of 100–150 minutes for five invitees, not measured time saved. Validate in a pilot.

Attendees
Value: Keep control of choices, booking and payment.
Capabilities: Indicate availability, choose available options, book and pay individually within provider terms.
Evidence: Real customer validation is still needed. The Module 4 classroom pilot figures were fictional illustrations, not research results.

AI-generated social asset: https://github.com/cugarguy/ps-go-to-market/blob/main/04-messaging/social-post.png

Copy across three surfaces

- Homepage headline: “Bring your friends together. Spend less time sorting out the details.”
Leads with: The value proposition. It puts the desired outcome first—getting friends together—then names the coordination burden Roamly Groups aims to reduce.
- Social post: “Getting friends together for an activity shouldn’t mean chasing every reply. With Roamly Groups, invite your friends, then let everyone share their availability, choose their options, and handle their own booking and payment.”
Leads with: The coordination frustration, followed by the capabilities. It starts with a recognizable problem and explains how each friend takes responsibility for their own steps.
- Email subject line: “One group outing. Everyone handles their own booking.”
Leads with: The capability of individual booking. It gives the initiator a specific reason to care: bringing the group together comes with fewer arrangements to manage personally.

Module 5
Pricing recommendation

Full pricing recommendation

Goal and model

Goal: Grow revenue from a known audience
Model: Free
Who pays: Each attendee pays for their own selected local experience at the applicable listed price and existing booking terms. The initiator pays only for their own participation. Groups coordination carries no additional fee at launch. Finance must verify that existing marketplace revenue covers the incremental coordination, payment-processing and support costs; no commission rate is assumed.

Tiers

Roamly Groups — Included: the recommended and only launch offering for informal friend groups, serving initiators and attendees together. $0 additional Groups coordination fee; experiences are still paid. Includes invitations, availability collection toward a shared date, activity options, individual booking and individual payment. Defer paid tiers and professional/corporate offerings until research demonstrates distinct needs and upgrade value.

Assumption to test

Including the complete Groups flow will cause enough additional completed group bookings to cover its incremental costs. Test with a controlled pilot against the existing workflow, measuring group-booking completion and contribution margin per eligible group attempt. Commission Max-Diff separately to rank capability value for initiators and attendees; it informs packaging, but does not establish willingness to pay or causal booking uplift.

Reflection

What I learned

Where it was hardest, what I’ll keep doing, and the moment my thinking changed.

Friction

Making decisions with limited evidence was the hardest part of building this strategy. I made the assumptions explicit and chose research to test them, including a controlled pilot for booking completion and economics and Max-Diff for capability priorities.

Key learnings

I will make assumptions explicit and choose research that tests the decision. I will also carry audience and value decisions consistently through positioning, messaging and pricing.

Aha moment

The same workflow needs different messages for initiators and attendees. The initiator values relief from coordinating everyone, while attendees value control over their own choices and payment.
